A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Proximal Diffusion Neural Sampler by the same authors. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and Appendices A–E are readable and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original PDNS experiments on continuous distributions, particle potentials, Ising/Potts models, and maximum-cut problems, including training and ablation results.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds alanine-dipeptide sampling, implementation comparisons, discrete scheduler ablations, and diagnostic analyses.

M1.justification: The proximal path-space updates, CE/WDCE objectives, and weighting/resampling algorithms are retained. The additional comparisons test existing variants; expanded notation and experimental stopping details do not establish a redesigned sampler.

E1.justification: Section 5.1 adds alanine-dipeptide conformational sampling with 22 atoms and 60 internal coordinates, substantially extending the molecular evaluation beyond idealized particle potentials. Maximum-cut graph-size coverage also changes from 20–32, 40–64, and 100–128 vertices to 16–20, 32–40, 64–75, and 100–128.

E2.justification: v2 Table 6 adds a Random comparator to maximum-cut results, where v1 Table 4 reported only PDNS. Existing synthetic, particle, and lattice comparator sets are unchanged. The alanine comparison uses PIS, DDS, AS, and ASBS, already evaluated elsewhere in v1.

E3.justification: Added protocols include alanine torsion-marginal KL evaluation using 10,000 samples and visualizations using one million samples. Appendix E.3 introduces 8×8 Ising scheduler tests with a fixed 10,000-epoch budget or adaptive progression after at least 100 updates and local ESS of 0.95. Existing benchmark training recipes remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds weighting-versus-resampling comparisons in Table 7, fixed/adaptive discrete scheduler sensitivity tests in Figures 13–14, and alanine initialization/failure analysis in Figures 10–11. Figures 19–20 add energy-distribution checks for Ising/Potts models. These extend the retained continuous ablations with several substantive diagnostic questions.

E5.justification: The original continuous tables retain their uncertainty values, and Figure 1 retains its two-run illustration. v2 adds no seed counts, repeated-run specifications, confidence intervals, or significance-testing procedures; the additional experiments do not introduce a new uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: v1 Tables 1–3 match v2 Tables 2, 3, and 5 numerically. Substantial new results include alanine torsion KL values of 0.02, 0.04, 0.03, 0.02, and 0.02 for PDNS, implementation/scheduler comparisons, and missed rare conformations. Maximum-cut scores are replaced under revised graph coverage and incompletely specified matching conditions, preventing a clean same-setting performance comparison.

T1.justification: Equation (3) explicitly states the fixed initial-marginal constraint. Appendix C.1 replaces its short proof with a conditional KL-chain-rule derivation and adds mathematical reasoning showing why non-memoryless references generally fail to produce the target terminal distribution. Proposition 3.1 and the principal proximal formulas remain unchanged.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions, and conclusion retain the same central claims: a unified continuous/discrete SOC framework, proximal training that mitigates mode collapse, and competitive sampling performance. Added experiments support these claims without redefining the main contribution.

C2.justification: Appendix D.4 newly acknowledges missed low-probability alanine modes, attributes them to initialization, and explains that proximal refinement may not recover absent modes. This materially qualifies the mode-coverage narrative. v2 also explicitly discusses failure without memorylessness and the energy-accuracy versus convergence-speed tradeoff between resampling and weighting.

D1.justification: v2 adds code-access information, OpenMM/internal-coordinate details for alanine, scheduler stopping settings, and an LJ-55 resource estimate of approximately 80 hours on one H100 using 14 GB. Conversely, the maximum-cut table drops v1's BA parameter m=4 and ER probability range [0.2, 0.8]. Existing hyperparameter tables are retained.

R1.justification: New references include Eastman et al. and Midgley et al. for the molecular evaluation, plus So et al. and Guo et al. for discrete adjoint samplers in Appendix A.2. The principal research positioning remains unchanged; numerous other reference edits merely update publication metadata.

P1.justification: v2 clarifies path-measure terminology and importance-weight explanations, standardizes energy notation and WDCE naming, and adds acknowledgments and publication/mentorship text. The overall section sequence and most existing prose remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds a notation table, alanine and implementation-comparison tables, and eight figures covering molecular diagnostics, scheduler tests, and energy histograms. The maximum-cut table is restructured into method rows with paired scores, while retained figures are resized or regrouped. These are substantial display changes beyond renumbering.

improvement.justification: The alanine evaluation, initialization failure analysis, and implementation/scheduler ablations strengthen empirical support and make applicability limits clearer. The expanded constrained proof and code-access information also help. These gains are incremental to an already extensive evaluation, and are partly offset by the lost maximum-cut generation parameters and less explicit paired-score labeling.
